home.intro: School readiness is a crucial phase in a child's development, encompassing a range of skills and competencies that prepare them for a smooth and successful transition into grade 1. The required sets of skills and abilities include cognitive skills such as basic literacy and numeracy, as well as emotional and social competencies like self-regulation, cooperation, and communication. A child who is school-ready can follow instructions, interact positively with peers and teachers, and adapt to the structured environment of a classroom. Ensuring school readiness involves a collaborative effort among parents, educators, and the community to provide enriching experiences and support that foster these essential skills.
home.closing: School readiness lays the foundation for a child's lifelong learning and success. A good early childhood education program should offer an age-appropriate and developmentally suitable learning environment for all children, ensuring that every 6-year-old is school-ready when they enter primary school. This tool will assist ECE educators in providing necessary early learning experiences to children based on their individual developmental journeys.

classification.name: Classification
classification.description: Classification is an important concept related to identifying different characteristics of things and categorizing them according to these characteristics. Children develop these skills by observing and examining different aspects of objects and identifying how these are alike or different.

levels.beginning: Unable to sort objects based on any characteristic
levels.progressing: Sorts objects based on any one characteristic
levels.advancing: Classifies objects based on any two characteristics
levels.schoolReady: Classifies objects based on three characteristics

patterns.name: Patterns
patterns.description: Understanding patterns is a foundational math skill upon which many mathematical concepts are based. For example, multiplication and counting both require an understanding of patterns. Patterns help children make logical connections between things, events, etc., by using their reasoning and problem-solving skills. Patterns can be found everywhere in our lives (e.g., the daily routine that we follow).

number-concept.name: Number concept
number-concept.description: Learning number concepts is one of the most important competencies and sets the foundation for understanding numbers. Number concepts involve a child’s ability to recognize numerals, one-to-one correspondence, counting and simple operations.

levels.progressing: Connects a number with an object and counts each object with understanding
levels.advancing: Identifies numerals and can link them with concrete objects
levels.schoolReady: Identifies both the smallest and the largest numerals within 1 to 10

seriation.name: Seriation
seriation.description: Seriation is an important concept related to measuring objects and categorizing them accordingly. At preschool age, children develop these skills for sequencing and putting objects in order, such as from smallest to largest, lightest to heaviest or least to most.

levels.beginning: Unable to compare two objects in terms of size, length, or quantity
levels.progressing: Compares two similar objects based on size, length, or quantity
levels.advancing: Arranges up to three objects by size, length, or quantity
levels.schoolReady: Arranges up to five objects by size, length, or quantity

vocabulary-and-expression.name: Vocabulary and expression
vocabulary-and-expression.description: Early vocabulary development is an important predictor of success in reading. A strong vocabulary enables a child to understand and communicate more effectively.

levels.beginning: Uses gestures to express/describe any event
levels.progressing: Uses words to express/describe any event
levels.advancing: Uses incomplete sentences to express/describe any event
levels.schoolReady: Uses complete sentences to express/describe any event

listening-comprehension.name: Listening comprehension
listening-comprehension.description: Listening comprehension is important for a child to understand what is being said. It includes a child’s receptive language skills as well as interpretation of what he/she hears.

levels.beginning: Does not pay attention to a story/conversation
levels.advancing: Understands a story/conversation – responds to simple/close-ended questions (e.g., what, when, who)
levels.schoolReady: Understands a story/conversation –responds to complex/open-ended questions (e.g., why and how)

emergent-reading--book-handling.name: Emergent reading – book handling
emergent-reading--book-handling.description: Book handling is a predictor of successful reading skills. It helps children to develop bonds with books, understand books, letters, words, and directionality, and to understand that print has meaning.

levels.beginning: Picks up books and explores them
levels.progressing: Identifies the cover page of a book

emergent-writing.name: Emergent writing
emergent-writing.description: Writing is an important skill. Between the ages of 3 to 6 years, children begin to learn to write, and by the time they are 6 years old, they should be able to write some simple words and/or their names.

levels.advancing: Engages in make-believe writing by using a combination of drawing and writing to express an idea
levels.schoolReady: Uses inventive spelling (based on phonics) to write words that are connected to a given topic

gross-motor-development.name: Gross motor development
gross-motor-development.description: Gross motor development involves large muscle movements in arms, legs and the torso, and includes skills, such as walking, running, climbing, throwing, kicking, and catching. A child needs considerable practice to develop gross motor skills.

levels.beginning: Limited balance in gross motor activities, e.g., jumping
levels.progressing: Maintains balance in gross motor activities
levels.advancing: Maintains balance and controls body while moving quickly
levels.schoolReady: Balances and coordinates well in a variety of activities, such as throwing a ball with aim or kicking a ball at a given target

fine-motor-development.name: Fine motor development
fine-motor-development.description: Fine motor development includes the development of small finger muscles and skills such as picking up things, threading beads, tying shoelaces, colouring within the boundary and stacking objects of different sizes.

levels.beginning: Limited coordination of small muscles in fine motor activities
levels.progressing: Maintains coordination of small muscles in fine motor activities
levels.advancing: Maintains coordination of small muscles while manipulating objects
levels.schoolReady: Controls and coordinates well in a variety of small muscle activities

interaction.name: Interaction
interaction.description: Interaction between young children and their peers and adults is important during the early years. Through interactions, children learn a language and social skills. Children who are given enough opportunities to interact and communicate through play-based activities tend to have a stronger social relationship with others.

levels.beginning: Plays alongside or near others but not with others
levels.advancing: Plays with others to make/create something jointly
levels.schoolReady: Engages in games with rules with other children

sharing-with-others.name: Sharing with others
sharing-with-others.description: Sharing is an important social skill. Children at an early age build these skills through observation.

levels.beginning: Shares unwillingly with peers and only when asked
levels.progressing: Begins to share selectively when encouraged
levels.advancing: Comes forward and shares with selected/few peers
levels.schoolReady: Comes forward and shares with all/any peers on her/his own

emotional-expression-and-regulation.name: Emotional expression and regulation
emotional-expression-and-regulation.description: Emotional regulation determines a child’s ability to express feelings and manage her/his emotions. Emotional regulation is a crucial skill for the well-being of the child. It is important that parents, caregivers and teachers provide support for the child’s emotional stability to help her/him grow and develop optimally.

levels.schoolReady: Gives appropriate response to her/his emotions

initiative.name: Initiative
initiative.description: Learning to take initiative is a behaviour that helps children navigate their lives with confidence. By taking initiative, children become more proactive and look for different ways to grow, study, excel and practice leadership skills.

levels.beginning: Does not take action even after being asked to do something
levels.progressing: Begins to take initiative when encouraged
levels.advancing: Takes initiative in some activities which she/he likes
levels.schoolReady: Takes initiative readily in most/all of the classroom activities

task-persistence.name: Task persistence
task-persistence.description: Task persistence is a skill that is important for children in classroom activities as well as in personal endeavours. It is important that children are encouraged to undertake challenging activities and tasks. This will help them learn to persevere, complete tasks and activities, and not give up.

levels.beginning: Focuses on play activities for a short period of time (about 5 minutes)
levels.progressing: Engages in play activities for about 10 minutes
levels.advancing: Sustains focus in play activities for about 15 minutes
levels.schoolReady: Sustains focus in play activities for at least 20-25 minutes, even if there are distractions

creative-expression.name: Creative expression
creative-expression.description: One of the best ways for children to learn about new concepts is to ignite their interest through hands- on experience. Besides giving young children the chance to explore different concepts through their senses, the experience helps develop other useful skills, including problem-solving and perseverance.

levels.beginning: Unable to create something to represent an idea or object (e.g., by using arts and crafts, dance or music)
levels.progressing: Creates something with an adult assistance
levels.schoolReady: Creates something innovative to represent an idea or object

imagination.name: Imagination
imagination.description: Imagination is the door to possibilities. It is where creativity and thinking outside the box begin in child development. Imaginative and creative play is how children learn about the world. During imaginative play, children manipulate materials, express themselves verbally and non-verbally, plan (intentionally or unintentionally), act, interact, react, and try different roles.

levels.beginning: Unable to answer questions about what would happen next in a story
levels.progressing: Answers questions about what would happen next in a story
levels.advancing: Role-plays characters in a story or uses props to tell a story
levels.schoolReady: Makes up and tells own story

beginning.label: Beginning
beginning.generic: The child shows initial attempts with limited success. Assess based on effort and support needed.

progressing.label: Progressing
progressing.generic: The child shows improvement with some support. Assess based on progress and guidance needed.

advancing.label: Advancing
advancing.generic: The child shows good understanding and application. Assess based on mastery and independence.

schoolReady.label: School Ready
schoolReady.generic: The child masters the task and applies it in context. Assess based on readiness for next stage.
